pages.title: About FontGen — Why a Fancy Text Generator With No Popups
pages.metaDescription: Why FontGen exists: every other fancy text generator buries the tool under ads and modals. This one doesn't. One ad, below the fold, and that's it.
pages.lede: Short version: every other one annoyed us, so we made this.
pages.bodyHtml:
The honest pitch

If you've ever searched for a fancy text generator, you know the drill. You land on a page, a cookie wall slides up, a newsletter modal pops over it, two ad blocks load above the actual tool, and the textarea you wanted is somewhere below a 'continue reading' fold. You came to convert one line of text. It takes 30 seconds and three dismissed dialogs.

FontGen is the version of that without the obstacle course. You type, the styles update, you copy one, you leave. There's a single ad unit further down the page — that's the whole business model — and nothing that interrupts you. No account, no 'allow notifications', no upsell.

How it works under the hood

None of this is a real font. Real fonts are files that change how text is drawn. What this does is swap your letters for different Unicode characters that happen to look like other fonts — the bold mathematical alphanumerics, the script set, the full-width Latin characters, and so on. Because the result is plain text, the styling travels with it wherever you paste it, even into an app that has no font options at all. The flip side: a few apps with locked-down fonts will show some of these characters as empty boxes, and there's nothing any tool can do about that — it's the receiving app, not the text. When you hit that, switch styles. Bold, Small Caps and Full-width render the widest.

What you can do with it

  • Style an Instagram, TikTok, X or Tumblr bio when the app gives you no formatting
  • Make a game name or Discord handle stand out
  • Add bold or italic emphasis somewhere there's no bold or italic button
  • Have a laugh with upside-down text, glitch text, or circled bubble letters

Who's behind it

A small team that builds web tools. We keep the surface area tiny on purpose — a handful of generators, done properly, instead of a hundred half-broken ones. If something's off, the contact page works.

pages.title: How Unicode 'Fancy Text' Actually Works (No, It's Not a Font)
pages.metaDescription: A plain explanation of how fancy text generators work — Unicode mathematical alphanumerics, combining marks, full-width characters — and why some of it breaks on certain apps.
pages.lede: The 30-second version, then the slightly longer one.
pages.bodyHtml:
The 30-second version

Your keyboard's letters are Unicode characters. So are thousands of other symbols that look like styled letters — a bold 'a', a script 'a', a circled 'a', a wide 'a'. A fancy text generator just substitutes one for the other. The result is still text, so it copies and pastes everywhere; it's just made of different characters than you typed.

The three tricks behind almost every style

1. Alternate alphabets (bold, italic, script, fraktur, double-struck, monospace, small caps)

Unicode has whole alternate sets of A–Z and a–z built for math notation — bold, italic, script, blackletter, double-struck, sans-serif, monospace. Generators map your letters onto these. Quirks: most of these sets are letters only, so numbers and punctuation stay normal. Some sets are incomplete (small caps is full, but the superscript and subscript 'alphabets' have missing letters that fall back to normal size).

2. Combining marks (strikethrough, underline, slashed, zalgo / glitch)

These styles don't replace your letters — they bolt extra invisible-on-their-own characters onto each one: a 'combining long stroke overlay' for strikethrough, a 'combining low line' for underline, and a big random pile of diacritics for zalgo. Your browser stacks them on. That's why zalgo can be made arbitrarily intense, and also why some apps cap or strip it — too many marks can break a chat layout.

3. Full-width and other 'shape' characters (aesthetic / vaporwave, bubble, squared, parenthesized)

These are characters that were designed wide (for mixing with Japanese kana) or inside a circle or a box. There's a full set of full-width Latin letters, a circled set, a squared set, a parenthesized set. Map your letters onto them and you get the spaced-out 'aesthetic' look or bubble letters.

Why it breaks on some apps

Two reasons. First, the app's font might not include a glyph for a particular character — so it draws the 'missing glyph' box (the little rectangle). Second, the app might deliberately reject certain Unicode ranges in fields like usernames, for moderation or layout reasons. Neither is something a generator can fix. The practical workaround is to pick a style built from the most common characters — Bold, Small Caps, and Full-width are the safest bets across the most apps.

Is it bad to use?

For a bio, a caption, a game name, a one-line joke — it's fine. For long passages or anything that matters for accessibility, it's a real problem: many screen readers announce these characters individually ('mathematical bold small a, mathematical bold small b...'), and search engines see gibberish, not styled text. So: short and intentional, yes. Your whole 'about me' paragraph or a web page heading, no — use real formatting there.

pages.title: Where Fancy Text Works: Instagram, TikTok, Discord, X & More
pages.metaDescription: Does fancy text work on Instagram, TikTok, Discord, X, WhatsApp, Roblox? A practical compatibility rundown — which fields accept it, which styles survive, and what to do when it breaks.
pages.h1: Where fancy text works (and where it doesn't)
pages.lede: A practical, app-by-app rundown. Last checked May 2026 — platforms change this stuff often.
pages.bodyHtml:
The short answer

Most styles work in most places, because it's all real Unicode. The exceptions are username fields (the strictest) and a handful of apps with limited fonts that render some glyphs as boxes. When in doubt, use Bold (sans), Small Caps, or Full-width — those survive the widest range of apps.

Instagram

Bio: yes — fancy text displays fine. Captions and comments: yes. Username (the @handle): the strictest field Instagram has — it rejects most combining-mark styles and some decorative ones. Story text uses Instagram's own fonts, so pasting fancy text there is hit-or-miss. If your username won't take a style, the bio almost always will.

TikTok

Bio and captions: yes, including full-width / 'aesthetic' text and small caps. Username: stricter, similar to Instagram. Comments: generally fine.

Discord

The most permissive of the lot. Messages: almost everything renders, including heavy decoration — though Discord caps extreme zalgo to stop layout abuse. Nicknames and 'About Me': most styles work; the very heavy combining-mark ones can get truncated. Custom status: usually fine. Note that Discord's own **bold** and ~~strikethrough~~ markdown works in messages but not in nicknames — that's where a Unicode bold/strikethrough comes in handy.

X (Twitter)

Posts: yes, all styles. Bio: yes. Display name: mostly yes, but it can trim or reject some combining-mark styles. Handle: can't be changed to fancy characters at all — handles are restricted to plain letters, numbers and underscores.

WhatsApp & Telegram

WhatsApp: works in messages, status text and 'About' — though rendering of combining marks varies between Android and iOS. Telegram: works in messages and bio; usernames are restricted.

Roblox, Fortnite, Free Fire, PUBG & other games

Highly variable, and they change their name filters often. The clean styles — Bold (sans), Full-width, Small Caps — pass most game name filters. Glitch / zalgo and stacked-mark styles usually don't. If a name bounces, drop to Bold and try again.

LinkedIn, Facebook, YouTube

LinkedIn: works in posts and headlines; strips it from some profile fields. Facebook: works in posts, comments and bio. YouTube: works in comments, channel descriptions and (mostly) channel names; community posts too.

When it shows as boxes

Those little rectangles mean the app's font doesn't have a glyph for that character. It's not corruption and it's not fixable from the tool side — pick a different style. The further down the 'exotic' scale a style is, the more likely you'll hit this. Bold and Small Caps almost never box out.

pages.title: All FontGen Generators — The Full List
pages.metaDescription: Every text and font generator on FontGen in one place: fancy text, cursive, bold, small, zalgo, upside down, bubble, aesthetic, Old English and more.
pages.lede: Everything we make, in one list. Pick a style and go.
pages.bodyHtml:
FontGen is deliberately small — a focused set of text and font generators, each one done properly, rather than a sprawl of half-working tools. They all share the same engine: type once, the chosen style updates instantly on the right, copy what you like. Here's the full lineup. (More on the way; we'd rather ship a tool that works than pad the list.)

How the generators are grouped

Under the hood the styles fall into a few families, and the dropdown on each tool groups them the same way:

  • Calligraphic — script, cursive, bold script, blackletter / fraktur, and small caps. The flowing, decorative letterforms. Letters only; no numbers.
  • Weight — bold and italic in their sans and serif variants. The safest set for getting past app font restrictions; bold sans renders almost everywhere.
  • Outline — double-struck and monospace. Clean, technical-looking letterforms with full numbers.
  • Decorative — full-width / aesthetic, circled bubble letters, squared letters, parenthesized, bracketed. The boxed-and-spaced looks.
  • Effect — strikethrough, underline, slashed, zalgo / glitch. These add marks to your existing letters rather than replacing them, so they layer on top of anything.
  • Misc — superscript, subscript, wide-spaced, dotted, upside-down, reversed. The odds and ends, including a couple of joke tools.

Which one should I use?

For a bio or caption, calligraphic and small caps read as the most deliberate. For a username or game tag, stick to Weight (bold) or full-width — they pass the most name filters. For a chat flex, the glitch and circled styles get the most reactions. And if a glyph shows as an empty box somewhere, that's the receiving app's font, not the tool — switch to Bold or Small Caps, which render the widest. There's a full app-by-app compatibility rundown if you want the specifics, and a plain explanation of how the whole Unicode trick works.

Not finding the one you want?

If there's a style you keep needing that isn't here — a specific symbol set, a regional alphabet effect, something — the contact page is open. We add styles based on what people actually ask for, not on keyword lists.

pages.title: Privacy — FontGen
pages.metaDescription: FontGen's privacy approach: the text you type never leaves your browser. What we do and don't collect, and what third-party ads see.
pages.lede: The text you type never leaves your device. Here's the rest.
pages.bodyHtml:
Your text stays on your device

Every generator on this site runs entirely in your browser. The text you type into the box is processed locally and is never sent to our servers — there are no servers involved in generating styles. The only thing stored is in your browser's local storage: which styles you've pinned as favorites and your light/dark preference. Clear your browser data and that's gone too.

What we collect

Basic, aggregate analytics — page views, rough geography, which generators get used — to know which tools to keep and improve. Nothing that identifies you personally, and nothing about the content you type.

Advertising

There is one ad unit on the page, served by a third-party ad network. Like most ad networks, it may use cookies or similar technology to show relevant ads and measure performance — that's the ad network's data collection, governed by its own policy, not ours. If you're in a region with consent requirements, you'll get a consent prompt for that. We don't sell data; we run one ad block and that's it.

Cookies

We don't set first-party tracking cookies. Local storage is used only for the favorites/theme preferences described above. The ad network and analytics provider may set their own — you can block those in your browser if you'd rather.

Contact

Questions about any of this go to the contact page.

This page describes our actual practices in plain language. For a specific legal jurisdiction's requirements, consult the policies of the analytics and ad providers linked from the consent prompt.

pages.title: Contact — FontGen
pages.metaDescription: Get in touch with FontGen — bug reports, style requests, broken renders, partnership questions.
pages.lede: Real inbox, real people. Mostly used for 'this style is broken on X app'.
pages.bodyHtml:
Get in touch

Email: {CONTACT_EMAIL}. That's the only channel — we don't run a support form, a live chat widget, or a Discord, on purpose. One inbox, read by an actual person.

What's worth sending

  • A style renders as empty boxes somewhere — tell us which style, which app, and which OS/version. Some of this we can fix (picking a more widely-supported character); some of it is the receiving app's font and there's nothing we can do — but we'd rather know than not. Screenshots help.
  • A style you want that isn't here — we add generators based on real requests, not keyword lists. Tell us what you'd actually use it for; that's the part that decides whether it gets built.
  • A bug — Copy button not working, the style dropdown misbehaving, layout broken on your device, the wrong result showing. Include your browser and device; it's almost always enough to reproduce it.
  • A correction — if something on the compatibility page or a how-to is out of date (platforms change their font handling constantly), point it out and we'll re-check and update the "last reviewed" date.
  • Partnership, press, or licensing — happy to hear it. Be specific about what you have in mind.

Response time

We aim to reply within a few business days. Bug reports and broken-render reports get looked at first because they affect everyone; feature requests get a slower, more thoughtful reply (or none, if it's something we've decided not to build — see below). If you don't hear back in a week, it's fine to send a nudge.

What we don't do

For the avoidance of doubt: we won't add "just one more" ad unit, gate any tool behind an email signup, run a newsletter, sell or share what you type (it never leaves your browser anyway — see the privacy page), or take requests to make a style "undetectable" by moderation systems. The no-popups, one-ad approach isn't a phase and it isn't up for negotiation. If you're looking for a white-label version or want to embed a generator elsewhere, that's a partnership conversation — use the email above.
